subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 12 periods = 480 minutes
Total: 12 periods · 8h 0min

section_titles: Fun at Vegetable Market — comparing weights
periods.activity_title: Heaviest to Lightest — comparing from experience

tasks_in_class.description: Look at pictures of animals and write their names from heaviest to lightest.
Write the name of the heaviest object in your home and explain how you know.
What is your weight? How did you know? Write your answer.
What do you think will be the weight of the half pumpkin? Write your estimate.

time_bands.activity: Children share what they carry to school and lift their bags; they talk about which feels heavier and why. The class then opens to Opening Q1, p.115 ("look at pictures of animals and write their names from heaviest to lightest....") — students rank animals and share reasoning.

Opening Q2, p.115 ("write the name of the heaviest object in your home and explain how you know....") — each child writes and then a few share their reasoning aloud. The class notices that knowing the heaviest object often comes from lifting effort, not from reading a number.
Opening Q5, p.115 ("what is your weight? How did you know? Write your answer....") — children reflect on how they found out their own weight and what kind of tool was needed.

Fun at Vegetable Market, p.115 ("what do you think will be the weight of the half pumpkin? Write your estimate....") — children study the scale image, estimate, and justify their guess. The class compares estimates and the teacher records the range on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Additional practice on school bag effort and heaviest book (Opening Q3–Q4, p.115) may be used as quick warm-up prompts if the class finishes early or assigned as written consolidation. A common error at this stage is confusing size with weight — children often rank a large light object as heavier; draw out examples where a small dense object outweighs a large hollow one.

section_titles: Kilograms and grams — fractions of a kilogram
periods.activity_title: Packets on the Pan — discovering gram-kilogram fractions

tasks_in_class.description: Estimate the weight of 6 bananas, 5 potatoes, 10 tomatoes, 15 onions as less/more than 1 kg; verify using a weighing balance.
Look at pictures: 2×500g=1kg so 500g=½kg; 4×250g=1kg so 250g=¼kg; 10×100g=1kg. Try doing the same with actual packets.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do, p.116 ("estimate the weight of 6 bananas, 5 potatoes, 10 tomatoes, 15 onions as less/more than 1 kg....") — in small groups children hold the produce or picture-reference it, make a prediction, and record. If a weighing balance is available, groups verify one item each.

Let Us Explore Q1 (a)(b)(c), p.116–117 ("look at pictures: 2×500g=1kg so 500g=½kg; 4×250g=1kg so 250g=¼kg; 10×100g=1kg....") — children study each pan-balance picture in turn, counting packets and reading the total, then complete the sentences. Where actual 500 g, 250 g, or 100 g packets are available, children replicate the balance.

The class reads aloud the three key relationships — 500 g = ½ kg, 250 g = ¼ kg, 100 g = 1/10 kg — and the teacher writes them in fraction and decimal form on the board. Children copy and add one real-life example next to each (e.g. a butter packet, a dry-fruit pouch).

periods.teacher_notes: Emphasise that ½ kg, ¼ kg, and 1/10 kg are not new 'rules to memorise' but conclusions the children just read from the balance pictures — the fraction language names the relationship they observed. A common error is writing 250 g = ½ kg because 'it sounds like half'; redirect by asking how many 250 g packets they counted on the pan.
materials: 500 g, 250 g, 100 g packet samples or replicas (if available)

section_titles: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
periods.activity_title: Balance, Tilt, and Match — reasoning with grams

tasks_in_class.description: How many 250 g packets balance one 500 g packet? Draw packets on the empty pan; complete: 250 g = ___ of 500 g.
Draw arrows to indicate which side the pan balance will tilt for each of the four pictures (a–d).
Match objects (baby, eraser, pen, books, table, fridge, etc.) to the units kilogram or grams.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Find Q1, p.117 ("how many 250 g packets balance one 500 g packet? Draw packets on the empty pan; complete: 250 g = ___ of 500 g....") — children first predict by reasoning from the fraction relationships they discovered for kilograms, then draw the packets and complete the sentence.

Let Us Find Q2, p.118 ("draw arrows to indicate which side the pan balance will tilt for each of the four pictures (a–d)....") — children study each picture, add the weights on each side mentally, and draw the tilt arrow. Pairs compare arrows and justify differences.

Let Us Find Q3, p.118 ("match objects — baby, eraser, pen, books, table, fridge, etc. — to the units kilogram or grams....") — children sort independently, then the class builds a shared two-column chart on the board. The teacher probes: 'How do you decide?' to surface the size-is-not-weight misconception.

periods.teacher_notes: Additional eraser-based computation tasks (Let Us Do Q1–Q3, p.119) and the Boxes of Sweet reasoning task (Let Us Think Q1–Q4, p.119) are strong follow-ups; use them as in-class extension or homework depending on pace. A common error in Q2 is adding grams and kilograms directly without converting — remind children to express all weights in the same unit before comparing.

section_titles: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching

tasks_in_class.description: How many erasers (each 10 g) will weigh the same as a 50 g Haldi packet?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Think Q1–Q4 (Boxes of Sweet), p.119
tasks_in_class.description: How many boxes of 500 g, 250 g, 100 g, and 50 g each are needed to pack 1 kg Kaju-katli? Write the number for each customer.

homework.description: A 100 g soap bar will weigh the same as _______ erasers (each 10 g).
_______ erasers will weigh the same as 250 g sugar.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q1, p.119 ("how many erasers — each 10 g — will weigh the same as a 50 g Haldi packet?...") — children hold a physical eraser, recall its 10 g weight, and reason how many are needed. The teacher writes the repeated-addition and division thinking side by side on the board.

Let Us Think Q1–Q4 (Boxes of Sweet), p.119 ("how many boxes of 500 g, 250 g, 100 g, and 50 g each are needed to pack 1 kg Kaju-katli?...") — children work through each customer's box size, connecting back to the fraction relationships from the kilograms and grams work. The class discusses whether their answers make sense by checking: does the number of boxes × box weight = 1 kg?

periods.teacher_notes: Let Us Do Q2 and Q3, p.119 (soap bar and sugar eraser problems) are assigned as homework tonight; they apply the same eraser-unit logic and consolidate the 10 g referent. A common error in the Boxes of Sweet task is writing the number of grams rather than the number of boxes — prompt children to re-read the question.

section_titles: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
periods.activity_title: Lifting and Estimating — weighing machines in daily life

tasks_in_class.description: Lift objects around you; write names of three you can lift easily and estimate their weights.
Write names of things you can lift with a lot of effort; estimate and write their weights.
Match objects (cat, elephant, 1-litre bottle, tiger, gas cylinder, pen, leaf, wooden chair) with estimated weight ranges.

time_bands.activity: The teacher displays or draws the five types of weighing machines from p.120 (pan balance, baby scale, kitchen scale, bathroom scale, luggage scale) and asks children which they have seen or used at home. Brief class discussion names where each machine is typically found and what it measures.

Let Us Do Q1, p.121 ("lift objects around you; write names of three you can lift easily and estimate their weights....") followed by Let Us Do Q2, p.121 ("write names of things you can lift with a lot of effort; estimate and write their weights....") — children move around the classroom, lift available objects (bag, book, pencil box, chair), categorise, and record estimates. Pairs compare whether their estimates agree.

Let Us Do Q4, p.121 ("match objects — cat, elephant, 1-litre bottle, tiger, gas cylinder, pen, leaf, wooden chair — with estimated weight ranges....") — children work individually, then the class builds consensus on the board. The teacher highlights that a 1-litre bottle of water weighs about 1 kg as a useful anchor for estimation.

periods.teacher_notes: The monthly consumption table (Let Us Do, p.120) is a home-enquiry task — children ask their parents about atta, rice, pulses, and sugar; note it in the teacher notes for parents if a communication goes home, or set it as an informal homework. A common error in Q4 is placing the gas cylinder in the lighter category because children associate 'cylinder' with small things — discuss that gas cylinders typically weigh 14–15 kg when full.
materials: Classroom objects of varied weight (bag, book, pencil box, chair)

section_titles: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
periods.activity_title: Packets by the Kilogram — converting bulk weights

tasks_in_class.description: How many 1 kg packets are in 10 kg, 20 kg, 50 kg, and 25 kg? Write the answers.

homework.description: Ask your parents: find the weight of atta, rice, pulses, and sugar consumed at home in a month; fill the table.

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with the Mirabai Chanu 'Do You Know' feature from p.121 — the class discusses the weights she lifts and connects this to what 25 kg or 50 kg feels like in terms of everyday packets they know (rice bags, flour sacks). This anchors the upcoming calculation in a real-world context.

Let Us Do Q3 (a–d), p.121 ("how many 1 kg packets are in 10 kg, 20 kg, 50 kg, and 25 kg?...") — children work through all four sub-parts, writing the multiplication or repeated-addition sentence alongside the answer. The teacher circulates and asks: 'How would you check your answer?'

Children share their strategies aloud: repeated addition, multiplication, skip counting. The class discusses which is quickest and whether all methods give the same answer, reinforcing the idea that different approaches are all valid and can be used to verify each other.

periods.teacher_notes: The monthly consumption table task (Let Us Do, p.120) is set as a home-enquiry task — children interview their parents and bring findings to the next sitting where the data can feed estimation discussion. A common error in Q3 is confusing 'how many packets' with 'how many grams' — emphasise that each packet is exactly 1 kg, so the question is simply how many 1s make the total.

section_titles: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
periods.activity_title: Containers and Capacity — less than, equal to, more than 1 litre

tasks_in_class.description: Find bottles/containers that hold less than 1 litre, exactly 1 litre, and more than 1 litre; write their names in the table.
How many 500 ml, 250 ml, 100 ml bottles fill a 1 l bottle? How many 250 ml in ½ l and 750 ml? How many 100 ml in ½ l and 800 ml?

time_bands.activity: Measuring Capacity (containers table), p.122 ("find bottles/containers that hold less than 1 litre, exactly 1 litre, and more than 1 litre; write their names in the table....") — children examine available containers (water bottles, mugs, jugs) or pictures, sort them into three columns, and fill the table. The teacher asks: 'How do you know this holds more than a litre?'

Let Us Find (a)(b)(c)(d), p.123–124 ("how many 500 ml, 250 ml, 100 ml bottles fill a 1 l bottle?...") — children work through each sub-part in order, pouring water if containers are available or reasoning from the pictures. They record the fraction relationships: 500 ml = ½ l, 250 ml = ¼ l, 100 ml = 1/10 l, mirroring what they found for grams and kilograms.

periods.teacher_notes: This section deliberately mirrors the kilogram-grams fraction structure from the weighing work — where children found that 500 g = ½ kg, they now find 500 ml = ½ l by the same reasoning. A common error is confusing a 500 ml bottle with a 1 litre bottle because both are 'big'; having a labelled 1 litre bottle as a physical reference helps.

section_titles: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
periods.activity_title: Dosing Cups, Droppers, and Daily Liquids

tasks_in_class.description: Find a 10 ml dosing cup; find how many 10 ml fill 100 ml, 250 ml glass, 500 ml vessel, and 1 l bottle.
Find out how much of these liquids are used at a time: eye drops, honey, cough syrup, cooking oil, and one more.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q1 (a–c), p.124 ("find a 10 ml dosing cup; find how many 10 ml fill 100 ml, 250 ml glass, 500 ml vessel, and 1 l bottle....") — children use a dosing cup (physical or referenced from their medicine kit drawing) and count or calculate the number of fills. The teacher writes the pattern on the board: 100 ÷ 10 = 10 cups, 500 ÷ 10 = 50 cups, and so on.

Let Us Do Q3 (a–e), p.124 ("find out how much of these liquids are used at a time: eye drops, honey, cough syrup, cooking oil, and one more....") — children draw on everyday knowledge, write their answers, and discuss why very small quantities (drops, ml) matter for medicines while litres are used for cooking. The class builds a rough sense of the range from 1 ml to 1 l.

periods.teacher_notes: The dropper activity (Let Us Do Q2, p.124) may be used as a quick extension for groups who finish early — it builds the 1 ml referent in the same way the eraser built the 10 g referent. A common error is confusing 10 ml with 10 l; ask children to picture their medicine spoon or dosing cup and check whether their answer is reasonable.

section_titles: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
periods.activity_title: Perfumed Oil Packing and Capacity Verification

tasks_in_class.description: Mr Krishna has 1 l perfumed oil; how many bottles of 500 ml, 200 ml, 100 ml, and 50 ml does each customer get?
Estimate and verify by measuring the capacity of: water bottle, glass, mug, jug, bucket, teaspoon, bowl.

homework.description: Visit nearby shops; make a list of different items sold in quantities 50 ml, 100 ml, 200 ml, 250 ml, 500 ml, 900 ml.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q4 (a–d), p.125 ("Mr Krishna has 1 l perfumed oil; how many bottles of 500 ml, 200 ml, 100 ml, and 50 ml does each customer get?...") — children apply the ml fraction relationships to a packing problem that parallels the Kaju-katli box task from the weighing work. They write a division sentence for each sub-part and check: does bottle size × number = 1000 ml?

Let Us Do Q5, p.125 ("estimate and verify by measuring the capacity of: water bottle, glass, mug, jug, bucket, teaspoon, bowl....") — children first write their estimates, then use available containers and water to verify. They record both estimate and actual value and note whether they overestimated or underestimated.

periods.teacher_notes: The shop-visit exploration (Let Us Explore, p.125) is set as homework — children note labelled quantities on product bottles at home or in a shop and bring the list to share. A common error in Q4 is dividing the number of millilitres rather than thinking about how many bottle-sized portions fit in 1 litre; grounding the question physically ('how many times does 500 ml go into 1000 ml?') helps.
materials: Assorted containers (water bottle, glass, mug, teaspoon)

section_titles: Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
periods.activity_title: How Much Water? — estimating and measuring daily use

tasks_in_class.description: How many litres of water do you drink daily? How much can a crow drink? How much milk do you drink? How much does an elephant drink?
How much water is used in: shower, watering crops, watering plants, washing clothes, and two more activities? Fill the table using given quantities.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Find (a–d), p.126 ("how many litres of water do you drink daily? How much can a crow drink? How much milk do you drink? How much does an elephant drink?...") — children estimate individually, then the class compares: the teacher writes a range on the board and discusses why humans and elephants need very different amounts. Standard milk-measuring cans (50 ml to 1000 ml) are referenced to help children visualise the quantities.

Let Us Find (activities table), p.126 ("how much water is used in shower, watering crops, watering plants, washing clothes, and two more activities?...") — children read the given quantities alongside the table and fill each activity's water use. The class reflects on which activity uses the most water and discusses simple ways to use less.

periods.teacher_notes: The activities table (p.126) gives children reference quantities — the teacher should clarify that these are typical amounts, not fixed facts, and that different households may use more or less. A common error is confusing 'litres per minute' with 'litres total' for shower water; prompt children to read the given quantity carefully before filling the cell.
materials: Standard measuring can (50–1000 ml) or picture of one

section_titles: Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
periods.activity_title: The Leaking Tap — measuring water waste and conservation

tasks_in_class.description: Put a container under a leaking tap for one hour; measure how much water is lost; calculate loss in a day and a week.

time_bands.activity: The teacher sets the scene: a tap drips slowly. Children predict — in millilitres — how much water a dripping tap might lose in one hour. Predictions are recorded on the board. Children briefly discuss how they might measure this: what container, what unit, how long.

Water Conservation activity, p.127 ("put a container under a leaking tap for one hour; measure how much water is lost; calculate loss in a day and a week....") — if a dripping tap or simulated drip is available, children collect and measure the water. Otherwise, the teacher provides a sample measurement (e.g. 150 ml in one hour) and children calculate: 150 ml × 24 = daily loss, daily × 7 = weekly loss. Calculations are written step by step.

Children compare their calculated weekly loss to known containers: 'Is this more or less than a bucket?' They then each write one sentence about what they would do to save water at home, connecting the measurement result to a conservation action.

periods.teacher_notes: This activity closes the capacity section and also reaches the chapter's conservation theme — the measurement skill and the real-world meaning are inseparable here. A common error in the multiplication step is multiplying by 7 before multiplying by 24 and getting confused; writing the calculation as two clear steps (hourly → daily → weekly) on the board prevents this.

periods.activity_title: Weigh It, Pour It — a whole-chapter market day

time_bands.activity: The class revisits the vegetable market scene that opened the chapter. Children name the two attributes the chapter explored — weight and capacity — and the key fraction relationships they found: 500 g = ½ kg, 250 g = ¼ kg, 100 g = 1/10 kg, and their exact mirrors for millilitres and litres. The teacher writes these as a shared reference on the board.

Market-stall estimation round: the teacher calls out objects and liquids in turn (a bag of rice, a bottle of oil, a packet of sweets, a medicine spoon of cough syrup, a bucket of water) and children hold up a 'kg / g' or 'litre / ml' card to name the right unit, then give a quick estimate. The class discusses choices, connecting back to the eraser-as-10-g referent and the 1-litre bottle as a capacity anchor.

Packing-problem challenge: the teacher poses two fresh scenarios on the board. (1) A sweet-seller has 2 kg of barfi; she packs it into 250 g boxes — how many boxes does she fill? (2) A shop has 2 litres of rose syrup; it is sold in 100 ml bottles — how many bottles does the shop fill? Children work individually, write a division sentence, and verify by checking that box-size × number = total. Pairs compare methods.

Quick whole-class check: the teacher reads four statements and children show thumbs-up or thumbs-down. (1) '250 g = ¼ kg.' (2) '500 ml = ½ litre.' (3) 'A fridge is measured in grams.' (4) 'A leaking tap can waste litres of water in a week.' Children briefly explain the two false statements, consolidating unit-selection and conservation ideas from across the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws on weight comparison and estimation from the vegetable market work, gram-kilogram and millilitre-litre fraction relationships, eraser-unit reasoning, pan-balance comparisons, weighing machine contexts, capacity pouring work, and water conservation measurement — the full arc of the chapter. No earlier activity or homework needs to have been completed for this unit to run; the teacher-posed scenarios and oral prompts are entirely self-contained. A common error at this stage is mixing units — adding grams to kilograms without converting — so the board reference list at the opening is a deliberate safeguard.
materials: Unit cards ('kg/g' and 'litre/ml') — one per child, prepared in this sitting from card slips

items.section_title: Kilograms and grams — fractions of a kilogram
items.prompt: A pan balance has 1 kg on one side. Which set of packets will exactly balance it?

options.label: A
options.text: One 500 g packet and one 250 g packet

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two 500 g packets, because 500 g + 500 g = 1000 g = 1 kg.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the gram values of the packets and check whether the total equals 1000 g.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student adds two different sub-units (500 g + 250 g = 750 g) but does not check whether the total reaches 1 kg, suggesting incomplete addition.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student multiplies 250 g × 3 = 750 g rather than 250 g × 4 = 1 kg, showing a recall error on the ¼ kg relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student picks five 100 g packets (500 g total) instead of ten, confusing ½ kg with 1/10 kg.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student place actual 500 g and 100 g packets on a balance and count. Stretch: ask what four different combinations of 500 g, 250 g, and 100 g packets also total 1 kg.

exercise.description: Estimate the weight of 6 bananas, 5 potatoes, 10 tomatoes, 15 onions as less/more than 1 kg; verify using a weighing balance.

items.section_title: Kilograms and grams — fractions of a kilogram
items.prompt: Look at a 250 g butter packet and a 1 kg flour bag. Write how many butter packets you would need to balance the flour bag, and explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Four 250 g butter packets, because 4 × 250 g = 1000 g = 1 kg.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the relationship 250 g = ¼ kg, so four quarter-kilogram packets make one whole kilogram.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw four equal boxes and write 250 g in each, then add. Stretch: ask how many packets are needed to balance 2 kg or 3 kg.

exercise.description: Look at pictures: 2×500g=1kg so 500g=½kg; 4×250g=1kg so 250g=¼kg; 10×100g=1kg. Try doing the same with actual packets.

items.section_title: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
items.prompt: Riya lifts her pencil box without any effort. Which is the most likely weight of her pencil box?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 200 g, because a pencil box is a small, light object that can be lifted easily.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the object's size and ease of lifting to a reasonable unit and magnitude from the weight scale studied.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses grams with kilograms for a small classroom object, placing it in the same range as a heavy bag of rice.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has no sense of scale; 2000 kg is heavier than a car.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student recognises kilograms as a weight unit but applies an unreasonably large number for a small object.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student hold the pencil box and then hold a 1 kg textbook; ask which is heavier. Stretch: ask the student to estimate in grams the weight of a full school bag and explain the difference.

exercise.description: Lift objects around you; write names of three you can lift easily and estimate their weights.

items.section_title: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
items.prompt: A shampoo bottle holds 200 ml. Which column in the capacity table does it belong to?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Less than 1 litre, because 200 ml is less than 1000 ml.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare 200 ml to 1000 ml (= 1 litre) and place accordingly.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student does not compare 200 ml to 1000 ml and may not know that 1 litre = 1000 ml.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be confusing the physical size of a shampoo bottle with a large container, or has no sense of the 1-litre benchmark.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses 200 ml with 500 ml (= ½ litre), a place-value or recall error.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: place a 200 ml cup next to a 1-litre bottle and ask which holds more. Stretch: ask the student to sort five containers (50 ml, 250 ml, 500 ml, 1 l, 2 l) into the three columns and explain each choice.

exercise.description: Find bottles/containers that hold less than 1 litre, exactly 1 litre, and more than 1 litre; write their names in the table.

items.section_title: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
items.prompt: How many 250 ml cups of water are needed to completely fill a 1-litre bottle?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the relationship 250 ml = ¼ litre, so four quarter-litre cups fill one litre.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw four equal sections on a picture of a 1-litre bottle and label each 250 ml. Stretch: ask how many 250 ml cups fill a 750 ml vessel.

exercise.description: How many 500 ml, 250 ml, 100 ml bottles fill a 1 l bottle? How many 250 ml in ½ l and 750 ml? How many 100 ml in ½ l and 800 ml?

items.section_title: Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
items.prompt: A tap drips and loses 200 ml of water in one hour. Write how much water is wasted in one full day (24 hours) and explain your calculation.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4800 ml in one day, because 200 ml × 24 = 4800 ml.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the hourly loss by 24 to find the daily total.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 24 boxes each labelled 200 ml and count in groups of five. Stretch: convert 4800 ml to litres and millilitres, and calculate the weekly loss.

exercise.description: Put a container under a leaking tap for one hour; measure how much water is lost; calculate loss in a day and a week.

items.section_title: Fun at Vegetable Market — comparing weights
items.prompt: A dog, a horse, and a sparrow are in a picture. Write their names in order from heaviest to lightest and give one reason for your order.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Horse, dog, sparrow — heaviest to lightest. A horse is a large farm animal much heavier than a dog, which is much heavier than a tiny bird like a sparrow.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare animals by size and lived experience to rank by weight.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to mime lifting each animal and describe the effort needed. Stretch: ask where a cat would fit in the order and why.

exercise.description: Look at pictures of animals and write their names from heaviest to lightest.

items.section_title: Fun at Vegetable Market — comparing weights
items.prompt: Arjun says his school bag is very heavy. Write two things that might make it heavy, and explain how you could find out which object inside is the heaviest.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two heavy objects might be a thick textbook and a water bottle. To find the heaviest, take each object out one at a time and compare — the one that feels hardest to lift in one hand, or sinks the pan of a balance the most, is the heaviest.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use lifting effort or a pan balance to compare objects one at a time.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to take two books from their own bag and hold one in each hand to compare. Stretch: ask how they could order all items in the bag from heaviest to lightest without a weighing machine.

exercise.description: Write the name of the heaviest object in your home and explain how you know.

items.section_title: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
items.prompt: One pan of a balance holds a 500 g packet. How many 250 g packets must be placed on the other pan to make both sides balance?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2 packets of 250 g, because 2 × 250 g = 500 g.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 500 g by 250 g, or use the relationship that 250 g is half of 500 g.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the balance and place labelled boxes on each side until they match. Stretch: ask how many 100 g packets would balance the same 500 g packet.

exercise.description: How many 250 g packets balance one 500 g packet? Draw packets on the empty pan; complete: 250 g = ___ of 500 g.

items.section_title: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
items.prompt: One pan holds 300 g of clay. The other pan holds 150 g of clay. Which way will the balance tilt?

options.label: D
options.text: The balance will not tilt at all

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Towards the 300 g side, because 300 g is heavier than 150 g.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the two weights; the heavier side pulls the pan down.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may believe lighter objects pull a balance down, reversing the logic of how a pan balance works.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may think that 150 g is half of 300 g and therefore 'balances', confusing equality of ratio with equality of weight.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may not understand that unequal weights always cause a tilt.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: demonstrate with two bags of different weight on a ruler balanced on a pencil. Stretch: ask how much more weight must be added to the 150 g side to make the balance level.

exercise.description: Draw arrows to indicate which side the pan balance will tilt for each of the four pictures (a–d).

items.section_title: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
items.prompt: Which object is most likely measured in grams rather than kilograms?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: An eraser, because it is a very light, small object and its weight is best expressed in grams.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the rule that small, light objects are measured in grams; heavy everyday objects are measured in kilograms.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not connected object size and heaviness to unit choice; a refrigerator weighs tens of kilograms.
what_each_option_reveals.C: A bag of rice is measured in kilograms; the student may be thinking of a very small quantity of rice.
what_each_option_reveals.D: A child's body weight is measured in kilograms; the student may be confusing size with lightness.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: hold an eraser in one hand and a textbook in the other; ask which feels more like a gram amount. Stretch: ask the student to write one more object measured in grams and one measured in kilograms, with a reason for each.

exercise.description: Match objects (baby, eraser, pen, books, table, fridge, etc.) to the units kilogram or grams.

items.section_title: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
items.prompt: A sweet-seller wants to pack 1 kg of peda into 250 g boxes. How many boxes does she need? Show your thinking.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the fraction relationship 250 g = ¼ kg, so four boxes make one whole kilogram.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw four boxes and label each 250 g; add them up. Stretch: ask how many 250 g boxes she needs for 2 kg, and for 1½ kg.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Think Q1–Q4 (Boxes of Sweet), p.119
exercise.description: How many boxes of 500 g, 250 g, 100 g, and 50 g each are needed to pack 1 kg Kaju-katli? Write the number for each customer.

items.section_title: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
items.prompt: Which animal most likely weighs more than 100 kg?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: An elephant, which weighs thousands of kilograms — far more than 100 kg.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the animal's known size to a reasonable weight range using estimation.

what_each_option_reveals.A: A cat typically weighs 3–5 kg; the student may not have a sense of what 100 kg feels like.
what_each_option_reveals.B: A hen typically weighs about 2–3 kg; the student may be confusing large birds with large weight.
what_each_option_reveals.D: A rabbit typically weighs under 5 kg; the student may be guessing without anchoring to a known reference.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: compare the weight of a gas cylinder (about 14 kg when full) to the animals and ask which is much heavier still. Stretch: ask the student to rank all four animals from lightest to heaviest and give an estimated weight range for each.

exercise.description: Match objects (cat, elephant, 1-litre bottle, tiger, gas cylinder, pen, leaf, wooden chair) with estimated weight ranges.

items.section_title: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
items.prompt: Priya uses about 5 ml of cough syrup each time she takes her medicine. Is 5 ml closer to a teaspoon or a full glass? Explain your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 ml is closer to a teaspoon. A teaspoon holds about 5 ml, while a full glass holds about 200–250 ml, which is much more.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the given quantity to known reference capacities — a teaspoon (~5 ml) and a glass (~250 ml).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show a teaspoon and a glass side by side and ask which feels like the right amount for medicine. Stretch: ask how many doses of 5 ml are in a 100 ml bottle of cough syrup.

exercise.description: Find out how much of these liquids are used at a time: eye drops, honey, cough syrup, cooking oil, and one more.

items.section_title: Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
items.prompt: Mohan drinks 2 litres of water every day. Which of the following is true?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: He drinks 2000 ml every day, because 1 litre = 1000 ml, so 2 litres = 2000 ml.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the relationship 1 litre = 1000 ml and multiply by 2.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may think 1 litre = 100 ml, a place-value error.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may think 1 litre = 10 ml, a much larger place-value error.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused litres and millilitres entirely, not recognising that 2 ml is a tiny drop.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show a 1-litre bottle and count how many 100 ml cups fill it, then ask how many millilitres that makes. Stretch: ask how many 250 ml glasses Mohan fills from his daily 2 litres.

exercise.description: How many litres of water do you drink daily? How much can a crow drink? How much milk do you drink? How much does an elephant drink?

items.section_title: Water use, conservation, and measuring containers
items.prompt: Look at the list of activities: watering plants, washing clothes, taking a shower. Write them in order from least water used to most water used, and explain how you decided.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Watering plants uses the least, then washing clothes, then taking a shower (or the shower and washing clothes may be swapped depending on the values in the table). The reasoning should refer to the quantities given in the activities table — larger quantities mean more water used.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the given quantities from the activities table and order them from smallest to largest.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the three quantities on the board and ask the student to arrange the numbers from smallest to largest. Stretch: ask which two activities together use more water than a shower, using the table values.

exercise.description: How much water is used in: shower, watering crops, watering plants, washing clothes, and two more activities? Fill the table using given quantities.

items.section_title: Comparing weights — pan balance and unit matching
items.prompt: Each eraser weighs 10 g. How many erasers weigh the same as a 70 g pencil pouch?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total weight by the weight of one eraser: 70 ÷ 10 = 7.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 7 boxes each labelled 10 g and count the total. Stretch: ask how many erasers weigh the same as a 130 g soap bar.

exercise.description: How many erasers (each 10 g) will weigh the same as a 50 g Haldi packet?

items.section_title: Weighing machines and real-life weight estimation
items.prompt: A sack of wheat weighs 25 kg. How many 1 kg packets can be filled from this sack?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total weight in kg by 1 kg to find the number of packets.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: count up in ones from 1 to 25 on a number line. Stretch: ask how many 2 kg packets can be filled from the same 25 kg sack, and whether there is any wheat left over.

exercise.description: How many 1 kg packets are in 10 kg, 20 kg, 50 kg, and 25 kg? Write the answers.

items.section_title: Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions
items.prompt: A shop has 1 litre of almond oil. A customer wants a bottle of 200 ml. How many such bottles can be filled from the 1 litre of oil?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert 1 litre to 1000 ml, then divide by 200 ml.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 5 bottles each labelled 200 ml and count: 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000. Stretch: ask how many 200 ml bottles can be filled from 3 litres of oil.

exercise.description: Mr Krishna has 1 l perfumed oil; how many bottles of 500 ml, 200 ml, 100 ml, and 50 ml does each customer get?
